title: The Waterfall That Walks Backward
blurb: Falling water eats the rock underneath it, so every waterfall slowly climbs upstream. Niagara has walked seven miles.

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Water runs down the river. The river comes to a cliff. The water does not stop. It falls. Down, down, down it goes. The water hits the rocks below. Splash. White foam jumps up. 2.subtitle: A reading sheet for ages 5 to 6

blocks.prompt: The Waterfall That Walks Backward
blocks.text: A waterfall starts as a river. The river runs along flat rock. Then the rock ends. The water tips over the edge and falls. At the bottom it lands hard. Year after year, the falling water digs a deep pool in the stone. That pool is called a plunge pool. The falling water also splashes back under the edge. It wears away the rock there too. One day the edge cracks and breaks off. The waterfall moves back a little. Then it starts again. A waterfall never stands still. It walks slowly backward, up its own river.

3.title: The Waterfall That Walks Backward
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: Hard Rock, Soft Rock
blocks.text: Not every rock is the same. Some rock is hard and stubborn. Some rock is soft and crumbles when water runs over it. A waterfall forms where a river crosses from hard rock onto soft rock. The soft rock wears away faster. Slowly the river carves a step, and the water begins to drop over the edge. Now the trouble starts. The falling water smashes into the bottom and digs a deep basin called a plunge pool. Spray curls back under the lip and eats at the soft rock hiding beneath the hard cap. After many years the hard cap has nothing left holding it up. It cracks. A slab of stone crashes into the pool. The waterfall is now standing a few feet farther upstream than it was. Then the whole thing begins again. Niagara Falls has been doing this since the ice age ended. It has moved about seven miles upstream and left a long gorge behind it, like a footprint.

notes: Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 3,212 feet

blocks.prompt: The Waterfall That Turns to Rain
blocks.text: In the jungle of southern Venezuela, flat mountains rise out of the forest with sides as sheer as walls. The Pemon people who live there call them tepuis. Rain falls on top of them, gathers into streams, and then arrives at the edge with nowhere to go but down. From the top of one of these mountains, Auyan-tepui, the water drops 3,212 feet. That is Angel Falls, the tallest uninterrupted waterfall on Earth. The main plunge alone, before the water touches anything at all, is 2,648 feet, nearly twice the height of the Empire State Building. Something strange happens on the way down. The fall is so long that the water cannot hold itself together. Air tears the stream apart, drop by drop. By the time it nears the bottom, much of it is no longer a waterfall at all. It is a drifting cloud of mist. In the dry season, visitors standing at the base do not get splashed. They get rained on, by water that left the cliff high above them many seconds earlier. The Pemon knew this place for centuries and called it Kerepakupai Meru. The name on most maps is much younger. In 1933 an American pilot named Jimmie Angel flew past the cliff while searching for gold. He came back in 1937, landed on the boggy summit, and sank his plane in the mud. He and his companions walked down off the mountain and out through the jungle over eleven days. The plane stayed up there for thirty-three years.

5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Victoria Falls sits on the Zambezi, between Zambia and Zimbabwe
Local name: Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders
About 5,600 feet wide and 354 feet tall
Spray can be seen from about 30 miles away
The zigzag gorges below are old waterfalls
Its mist grows a rainforest that rain alone could not

blocks.prompt: The Smoke That Thunders
blocks.text: The Zambezi River spends hundreds of miles doing nothing dramatic. It slides across a broad, flat sheet of dark basalt on the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, wide and unhurried, and gives no warning at all. Then the ground opens. The whole river, more than a mile across, drops 354 feet into a crack in the earth. This is Victoria Falls. It is not the tallest waterfall in the world, and it is not the widest. It is something better: the largest single sheet of falling water anywhere, because it is the only place where a river this wide falls this far all at once. The people of the region named it long before any map did. They called it Mosi-oa-Tunya, which means the smoke that thunders, and both halves of that name are earned. The spray climbs more than a thousand feet into the air and can be seen from roughly thirty miles away, standing over the flat country like a column of smoke from a fire that never goes out. The sound arrives before you do. Now look at where the water goes, because that is the real story. The chasm it falls into is barely four hundred feet wide. A river of more than a mile has to escape through a gap narrower than a few city blocks, and it does this by turning hard and squeezing out through a churning throat called the Boiling Pot. Below that, the gorge zigzags. It cuts sharply left, then sharply right, then left again, over and over, for miles. Those zigzags are not decoration. Each one is a former Victoria Falls. The basalt is threaded with long cracks, and the river finds a crack, pours into it, and works backward along it until the whole line has been opened into a new chasm. Then the falls jumps to the next crack and begins again. There are at least seven abandoned gorges downstream, and each one held the waterfall for thousands of years before the river moved on. Victoria Falls is not where it started and it is not where it will end. It is simply where the river has got to. Somewhere upstream, in rock that looks perfectly ordinary today, is the crack that will be the next one.

6.title: The Waterfall That Walks Backward
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Geologists call the lip of a waterfall a knickpoint
Niagara has retreated about seven miles since the ice age
The Niagara Gorge is the track it left
Waterfalls isolate fish populations above and below
Hawaii's rock-climbing goby scales cliffs with a pelvic sucker
Earth's largest waterfall is underwater, in the Denmark Strait

blocks.prompt: A Waterfall Is Not a Place
blocks.text: Point at a waterfall and you are pointing at an event, not an object. The rock you are looking at will not be there in a few thousand years, and neither will the falls. Geologists do not have a word for waterfall in the way a tourist does. They have a word for the lip: knickpoint. A knickpoint is a break in a river's profile, a place where the slope suddenly steepens, and a river spends its entire existence trying to erase them. Here is how the erasing works. A river running over hard rock that sits on softer rock will eventually expose the soft layer at some downstream edge. Soft rock loses. It washes out, undercutting the hard cap above it until the cap has nothing beneath it but air. Then the cap breaks. A slab drops into the plunge pool, the lip retreats upstream, and the process resets and runs again. Every waterfall you have ever seen is a machine engaged in destroying itself. Niagara supplies the arithmetic. When the last ice sheet withdrew roughly twelve thousand years ago, the falls stood near what is now Lewiston, New York. It has since chewed about seven miles south, and the Niagara Gorge is the trench it left behind. That gorge is not a valley the river happened to find. It is the waterfall's track. Left alone, Niagara would eventually reach Lake Erie and quietly begin draining it. Engineers have slowed the retreat by diverting much of the flow through power stations, which is a strange thing to sit with: we have put a waterfall on a leash, partly to keep it from eating a Great Lake. Waterfalls do not only move. They divide. A fish that cannot get up one is locked out of every mile of river above it, and populations kept apart for long enough stop being one population. Hawaii offers the rebuttal. A fish called the Nopili rock-climbing goby hatches, washes out to sea, and then comes back and climbs. It grips wet rock with a sucker formed from its fused pelvic fins and hauls itself up cliffs hundreds of times its own body length, using the same mouth muscles it uses to scrape algae off stone. The waterfall is a wall, and the goby simply went up it. The largest waterfall on the planet, meanwhile, has never been photographed and nobody has heard it. It is in the ocean. Between Greenland and Iceland, freezing dense water from the Nordic Seas pours south over an underwater ridge and sinks beneath the warmer, lighter Atlantic. This is the Denmark Strait cataract, and it descends nearly eleven thousand five hundred feet. Estimates put its flow near three million cubic meters every second. Niagara, at full strength, moves about two thousand four hundred. No one built a viewing platform, because there is nothing to see. The water is falling through water. So decide what a waterfall actually is. It is not the water, which is different water every instant. It is not the rock, which is on its way out. It is the shape that a long argument between the two makes while the argument is still being settled.

(a break in a river's profile where the slope suddenly steepens; rivers work to erase them; cite: a river spends its entire existence trying to erase them)
(soft rock washes out, undercuts the hard cap, cap breaks, lip retreats, repeat; machine because it runs the same cycle over and over automatically)
(at Waterfalls do not only move. They divide; two short sentences signal the pivot)
(a rebuttal to the claim that waterfalls divide populations absolutely; earned, because the goby climbs the barrier and crosses it)
